data.title: Methods for bringing dynamic mediums to physical reading contexts
data.contentMarkdown:
# Methods for bringing dynamic mediums to physical reading contexts

One response to [[z2bSwDuxY2Jbv1ntLKB3SL1:::Reading texts on computers is unpleasant]] is to give up, to invert the problem: how to bring the properties of dynamic mediums to physical books?

*   Projectors / cameras (a la [[zDpmsw9zxmk2eXsoHVUqidf:::Dynamicland]])
    *   I like the notion of a wide-angle camera you can clip onto a book, just like you might clip on a little light for reading at night.
*   Treat a phone or tablet as a “companion device”—it’s not where the reading happens, but it’s perhaps where dynamic supports appear.
*   [[zWG9EgWoprv9cbXXkhg8YNS:::Voice-based interface]]
    *   [[zJxuTHe8PCELxMWhvzVxT8t:::Specifying book passages with a few spoken words]]

## References

My thinking on this topic was informed by a series of generative sessions with [[Derrek Chow]] in late 2022.

backlinkedNotes.linkingNoteTitle: Specifying book passages with a few spoken words
contextBlocks: [[zWG9EgWoprv9cbXXkhg8YNS:::Voice-based interface]] offers one avenue for [[z2vMujPz4bgD3BwtwbU9U9B:::Methods for bringing dynamic mediums to physical reading contexts]]. Many dynamic interactions involving a text will require you to indicate a passage of interest in the text, or to know what you’re looking at. For instance, maybe you’d like to make a note about a passage, or highlight it, or add a memory system prompt about it. How to do that with voice?
